actualCourseEvidence.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
actualCourseEvidence.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
actualCourseEvidence.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.

actualCourseEvidence.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community

actualCourseEvidence.description2: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.

actualCourseEvidence.methods: Close life-narrative analysis; Smith and Watson's strategies for reading life narratives; Theory-guided analysis of memory, identity, embodiment and agency; Comparative textual and contextual interpretation; Structured autobiographical creative writing

actualCourseEvidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
actualCourseEvidence.name: Ethics
actualCourseEvidence.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
actualCourseEvidence.discipline: Moral philosophy; Metaethics; Practical ethics
actualCourseEvidence.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
actualCourseEvidence.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

actualCourseEvidence.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
actualCourseEvidence.name: Media & Race
actualCourseEvidence.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
actualCourseEvidence.discipline: Cultural history; Media studies; Race and ethnicity studies; American studies
actualCourseEvidence.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
actualCourseEvidence.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

actualCourseEvidence.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
actualCourseEvidence.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
actualCourseEvidence.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
actualCourseEvidence.discipline: Sociology; Social theory; Civil society studies
actualCourseEvidence.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
actualCourseEvidence.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design

frozenConceptsBeforeSelection: Retain two questions: material evidence/textual history with physical landscape methods; institutional/community interpretation of heritage. Rebuild weak contributions under those existing evidenced questions, rather than adding interests from the UCR inventory.
closestChallenge: Programme-level object/material-evidence backbone includes WorldArchaeology catalogue/drawing/local material hypothesis work, Greek archaeology, ancient democratic heritage, art/source interpretation and material-media archaeology. DynamicEarth geological mapping/stratigraphy and soils/GIS add real landscape methods. This is meaningful archaeological/material-culture study, not a claim that all24courses are ancient archaeology.
relatedChallenge: Eight art/heritage courses with material-media work connect archaeological/ancient objects, restitution, curatorial narratives and institutional interpretation to qualitative inquiry, Indigenous public-history collaboration, life-memory narratives, civil-society power and ethics. The response is a substantive heritage/public-memory choice supported by target generators, not a generic communications composition.
selectionsAndTrace: Chemical, thermodynamic/mechanical and elementary modelling foundations, with biopolymer preparation/measurement, support the later environmental soil and geospatial investigation of landscape evidence. These are real scientific foundations and laboratory skills, not archaeological materials science.

Studies late-medieval/Renaissance to contemporary Western art, with close painting analysis, on-site artwork study and evidence-based art-historical interpretation. This is a concrete visual-source and museum-context foundation, not ancient artefact or excavation training.
examines the formation and decline of empires, including the political structures within which Mediterranean and European material cultures developed

Actual artefact measurement/cataloguing, technical drawing, craft interpretation, archaeological database/literature research and a contemporary material-evidence project directly implement object-based archaeology. No full excavation sequence is inferred.
directly studies Greek archaeology and reconstructs community and democratic decision-making from material remains
reads major texts from Gilgamesh onward, supplying written cultural evidence that can be interpreted alongside material remains
examines ancient myths and epics across cultures and how they shaped later cultural memory
teaches data cleaning, visualisation and work with spatial data as general digital methods relevant to documenting and analysing evidence, without claiming digital archaeology
treats historical media technologies as material objects whose physical properties shape the circulation and preservation of knowledge

Actual rock/mineral observation, stratigraphy, geological mapping, cross-sections and Ardennes field reporting develop landscape/material field evidence. These are substantial geological methods, not archaeological excavation or finds processing.
provides hands-on GIS, remote-sensing and drone-data analysis relevant to historical landscapes while remaining environmental rather than archaeological field training

Uses soil coring, field/laboratory soil chemistry, microscopy, ICP interpretation and seismic/resistivity/electromagnetic surveys to characterize soils and aquifers. Specific complementary methods for landscape/subsurface evidence, not a substitute for archaeological excavation or dating.
follows warfare, weapons and military organisation from Greek and Roman antiquity onward, adding historical interpretation of material technologies
examines heritage, colonial acquisition, looting and repatriation through African art and museum collections
connects ancient Greek material culture and democratic practice to their contested modern heritage
examines museums, curatorial practice and exhibition strategies as institutions through which material heritage is interpreted

Studies Greek and Roman rhetorical history, original persuasive techniques, argumentation, debates and speeches. These give specific classical-text interpretation and public-explanation practice for the material-culture/heritage concepts; a heritage project is not guaranteed.

Interprets political thought from classical antiquity onward through original texts, historical contexts and comparative argument. It supports interpretation of ancient community, authority and democratic heritage rather than an archaeology theory sequence.
Art-historical historiography from the16thcentury to present and its interpretive methods; not archaeological excavation publication training.

Current Researching the American Century teaches research-question formulation, critical source engagement, methodological rigour and a substantial historical research paper. Provides specific historical-research process skills; neither a Walcheren expedition project nor ancient-source/excavation research is assumed.
combines critical study of documentary form with producing a short documentary for wider audiences
supplies the modern political and social history within which museums, national heritage institutions and public uses of the past developed

Uses Indigenous storywork, historical sources, relational accountability and public-history multimedia collaboration to examine whose histories are represented and how communities participate. A specific public-memory/restitution complement, without claiming European excavation or museum training.

Studies social boundaries, identity, stratification and exclusion through historical sociological theory and an evidence-based social-problem paper. These provide specific frameworks for evaluating institutional representation and community inclusion; a heritage topic is not guaranteed.
teaches qualitative research into meaning, power and public experience, supporting audience and community research in heritage settings

Analyzes memory, identity, trauma, ethics and autobiographical truth in memoir/diary/travel narratives, with an independent life-narrative project. Supports interpretation of remembered lives and public narratives rather than archaeological material analysis.
provides ethical frameworks for questions of ownership, restitution, stewardship and obligations to past and present communities

Studies institutions, public spheres, hegemony, solidarity and decolonial civil-society theory, then researches an organization or movement. This informs institutional authority and community participation in heritage interpretation; a heritage case topic is not guaranteed.

schedules.label: Archaeology, art & historical interpretation
schedules.concept: Studies past societies through actual artefact analysis, world and Greek archaeology, ancient democratic heritage, art, history and literary sources. Geological field mapping, soil analysis and GIS add specific landscape and material-evidence methods. Philosophical and rhetorical texts support interpretation of ancient communities. Modern art and historical research broaden the composition; they do not become ancient archaeology. This is a qualified material-culture response, with substantial gaps in the European period sequence, archaeological excavation, archaeometry and an archaeology thesis.
schedules.labelReason: The completed composition combines archaeology with substantial art, historical/textual interpretation and environmental methods. The label represents that combination rather than calling all24 courses ancient-society or archaeological study.
progression: All actual offerings/prerequisites pass. Gateway precedes Earth Observation. First-year archaeology/art/literature foundations precede advanced museums, heritage and interpretation. Dynamic Earth in semester3 precedes the semester4 soil/GIS field-method complement. Historical research in American Century is generic historical-method preparation, not an ancient-source project. Six300-level courses and Year1 PPD.

schedules.label: Cultural heritage, museums & public memory
schedules.concept: Studies how material culture and cultural memory are interpreted, displayed and contested. Archaeology, Greek democratic heritage, African heritage and restitution, museum/curatorial analysis and art-historical methods form the object-based core. Indigenous public-history work, racial representation, life narratives, qualitative inquiry, decolonial civil-society theory and ethics support specific questions of whose histories institutions tell and how communities participate. Documentary and classical rhetorical practice provide public interpretation tools; these are not archaeological field or heritage-management qualifications.
schedules.labelReason: The completed curriculum concentrates on museums, heritage ethics, public memory, restitution, community interpretation and documentary communication. The label reflects that institutional and public-facing emphasis.
progression: All actual offerings/prerequisites pass, with nine advanced courses and Year1 PPD. Art/archaeology foundations precede advanced heritage and museums; sociology precedes advanced civil-society theory. Primary/public-history, memory narrative and qualitative research support public interpretation with no guaranteed archaeological project subject.
schedules.distinctness: The programmes share16courses and each has8unique courses/60EC. The first prioritises ancient literary/political interpretation and physical landscape/GIS/data methods; the second replaces that strand with public history, life narratives, sociology/qualitative inquiry/civil-society theory and ethics. This changes the research object and methods used to interpret institutional and community heritage, beyond the numerical floor.

repairs: Replace first-programme generic philosophy with actual geological field methods, modern-history context with classical political texts and race-media context with classical rhetoric. Replace second-programme fictional stylistics, primary-school rhetoric and sustainability persuasion with public history, life narratives and civil-society theory. These changes improve concrete academic contribution as well as repairing the invalid2028h1RhetoricInAction offering. Correct ResearchingAmericanCentury from current description2; do not use archivedWalcheren or reconstruct enrichment.
feasibility: Both24unique/180EC/4persemester/Year1PPD. Six/nine advanced courses. All current formal prerequisites and covered-term offerings read and verified; gateway before EarthObservation. Introductory art/archaeology precedes advanced heritage; geological foundations precede soils/GIS; sociology precedes advanced social theory. No extra formal progression constraint invented.
distinctness: 16shared;8unique/60EC in each. Physical/geospatial/data and ancient textual/political methods versus institutional/community history, sociology/qualitative inquiry, memory narrative and ethics.

candidateStopping.label: Excavation, archaeological science & field investigation
candidateStopping.assessment: Actual UCR archaeology includes artefact cataloguing/drawing and a small material-evidence project; Dynamic Earth adds stratigraphy and geological field mapping, and Soils & Aquifers adds real coring, geophysical surveys and analytical laboratory methods. These are fully credited. They still do not construct a sustained archaeological excavation/finds-processing/chronometric or archaeometric sequence sufficient to organize another24-course response. This is a substantive disciplinary-construction limit, not missing offering coverage.

fieldScienceChallenge: ActualUCR cataloguing/drawing, local material collection, geological stratigraphy/mapping, soil coring, ICP interpretation and geophysical surveys fully credited. They still do not supply a sustained archaeological excavation/finds-processing/dating/archaeometry sequence for another coherent24-course route. A third generic physical-science curriculum would not respond sufficiently to the archaeological object and specialist method.
